publicationTitle: 2024 14th International Workshop on Resilient Networks Design and Modeling (RNDM)
abstract: In this paper we look at the benefits of using network sharing (NS) in radio access networks (RAN) for resilience to hardware or software faults, or, more generally, to down times due to faults, network upgrades, scheduled maintenance and the like. By network sharing we mean that customers of two (or more) mobile network operators (MNOs) can access network infrastructures regardless of their subscription, thanks to a NS agreement between the MNOs. This implies that whenever an equipment is down in one of the MNO infrastructures, customers can rely on the equipment within another infrastructure to obtain their services, as long as the capacity of the non-faulty RANs is sufficient to serve all traffic in the area interested by the fault. By so doing, the equipment down is concealed from end users for the whole down duration. Using real data for mobile data traffic and base station (BS) positions, we estimate the fraction of time during which faults can be concealed from end users as a function of fault duration, as well as the fraction of traffic that is denied service due to faults that cannot be concealed due to scarcity of resources in the non-faulty RAN(s). Our results show that network sharing succeeds in concealing a large fraction of equipment downs, and that the fraction of lost traffic is small, assuming reasonable fault duration.

articleTitle: Analyzing Network Routing Resilience: A Hybrid Approach of Face and Tree Routing
publicationTitle: 2024 14th International Workshop on Resilient Networks Design and Modeling (RNDM)
abstract: With the aim of ensuring reliable and consistent communication, network topologies need to be able to correctly and rapidly respond to potential errors. Through these responses, the connection within the network is maintained, even in the presence of faults. This is achieved through various mechanisms, known as fast failover algorithms, which are implemented in the data plane, opposed to the slower control plane. In this work, an established fast failover approach, which routes through trees, is extended. This extension is achieved by dividing the routing path into two parts and using both face routing and tree routing for forwarding packets. This is done against the backdrop that Tree Routing yields suboptimal results when the source of the routing is highly error-prone. To counteract this, this work proposes a modification of the Tree Routing by first routing through a waypoint using face routing and then utilizing tree routing. As such, the routing is resilient to errors both at the source and destination. Results of this work showed in a setting of clustered failures using real world graphs, resilience can be enhanced, with a higher hop count due to utilizing the faces to circumvent early failures. Furthermore, it has been shown that for random errors in random graphs, the resilience is also increased compared to the original tree routing algorithm.

articleTitle: Higher-Order Graph Models in Network Security
publicationTitle: 2024 14th International Workshop on Resilient Networks Design and Modeling (RNDM)
abstract: Security engineering has shifted from the paradigm of securing a list of assets to defending interconnected graphs. In this new paradigm, security researchers have employed higher-order graphs such as directed hypergraphs, where nodes represent sets of elements, and directed edges connect these sets. Higher-order graphs are unmatched in their flexibility to naturally model a broad range of network systems where higherorder relationships exist among their interacting parts. Despite their powerful expressiveness, higher-order graphs have been underexplored in the security modeling literature because of their inherent complexity and the lack of appropriate tools and algorithms. In this paper, we give an introduction to various types of higher-order graphs, including metagraphs, directed hypergraphs, and explore their relationships with similar concepts such as Petri nets. We also present the applications of higherorder graphs in a couple of network security modeling problems with recently developed algorithms for analyzing these types of graphs.

articleTitle: Resource Efficiency and Survivability of Network Slice Isolation Strategies After Massive Outages
publicationTitle: 2024 14th International Workshop on Resilient Networks Design and Modeling (RNDM)
abstract: The increasing digitalization of various industries requires communication services tailored to specific needs. Providing these services on a shared communication infrastructure is challenging because the performance, dependability, and security requirements are heterogeneous and sometimes even conflicting. The new generations of mobile networks (5G/6G) will enable the provision of separate, isolated, customized communication services through network slicing, which can have different requirements. The isolation of service provisioning is needed to protect critical services. This paper focuses on how varying degrees of network slice isolation will protect and restore critical services in case of massive outages. We implement alternative network slice isolation to study the trade-offs between resource utilization and the performance of communication services. Specifically, we conduct a survivability assessment of the isolation strategies during and after a massive outage caused by software bugs and cyber-attacks. The main observations show how stricter isolation methods decrease resource utilization and network performance in regular operations due to constraints on resource allocation. On the other hand, the study shows that isolation methods significantly benefit critical slices during massive outages, illustrating a system's vulnerability to internal threats such as software bugs and intentional cyber-attacks.

articleTitle: Local Fast Failover Routing on Directed Networks
publicationTitle: 2024 14th International Workshop on Resilient Networks Design and Modeling (RNDM)
abstract: The fast and resilient routing of packets in networks presents a complex problem with high practical relevance due to its application in local/wide area networks and the Internet in general: nearly all modern communication networks implement some form of re-routing to retain connectivity after failures. Therefore a lot of research regarding this problem has been conducted, but it is almost exclusively focused on the prevalent case of undirected networks. In this paper we hence provide an overview of the current research concerning fast rerouting algorithms and the unique challenges of re-routing on directed graphs, in particular the transferability of existing algorithms to this special case. Subsequently, one of these algorithms, called Keep Forwarding, originally designed for undirected graphs, is adapted for directed graphs and then evaluated against other algorithms in a simulation on synthetic (random and disk graphs) and real-world (from the Heathland sensor network experiment) topologies. We show that our adaptation is superior to the other algorithms on most topologies, with the average packet loss and stretch being up to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$61 \%$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$65 \%$</tex> lower than the second-best respectively on the real-world topology.

articleTitle: Fronthaul Resource Optimization for Cell-Free Massive MIMO Networks
publicationTitle: 2024 14th International Workshop on Resilient Networks Design and Modeling (RNDM)
abstract: Cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (mMIMO) is expected to be a key technology in 6G and beyond networks where User Equipments (UEs) are jointly served by multiple Radio Units (RUs) in order to enhance the throughput and reliability. This joint cooperation leads to a significant increase in fronthaul (FH) resource requirements as UE traffic has to be routed simultaneously between multiple RUs (constituting the so-called RU cluster for a UE) and a cluster processor (CP) located at a Distributed Unit (DU) site. In this paper we propose a novel two-step algorithm for FH network resource optimization with the objective to balance the traffic load on the FH links and the processing load at the DU sites. In the first step, we determine the cluster specific traffic for a given UE/traffic density distribution within the coverage area and a given cluster formation scheme using a Monte Carlo approach. For the second step, we formulate a mixed integer linear programming (MILP) optimization problem to balance the FH link loads and the processing loads at the DU sites - i.e. we solve the FH traffic routing and CP placement problem. Finally we apply our method on a cell-free O-RAN example scenario and investigate the impact of different configuration parameters on the optimization results. Our approach provides a generalised way to optimize FH resources in user-centric cell-free massive MIMO network deployments.

articleTitle: Shared Backup Path Protection with QoT Guarantee in Elastic Optical Networks
publicationTitle: 2024 14th International Workshop on Resilient Networks Design and Modeling (RNDM)
abstract: Shared backup path protection (SBPP) mechanisms can be utilized to effectively protect elastic optical networks (EONs) against any single link failures, offering numerous advantages over other protection techniques. However, maintaining the quality-of-transmission (QoT) in EONs after the recovery process in the presence of physical layer impairments is a complex task, mainly due to the different interference patterns that appear when different links fail. To address this issue in SBPPbased EONs, this work proposes a mixed integer linear program (MILP) where candidate working paths are pre-computed in a pre-processing step, while the backup paths for each demand are computed within the MILP. The proposed MILP ensures that the QoT remains above a predetermined threshold in both the working and backup paths of each demand, for both the normal and single link failure operation scenarios.

articleTitle: On the Resilience of Mutually Dependent Power and Data Networks
publicationTitle: 2024 14th International Workshop on Resilient Networks Design and Modeling (RNDM)
abstract: A vital requirement of the power system is always to maintain a balance between generation and demand. Distributed renewable energy sources are being integrated into the power grid to meet the increasing demand and simultaneously decrease the power grid's carbon footprint. These sources are characterized by their unpredictability regarding generation output and direction of power flow. This rising unpredictability threatens the system's resilience. Information and communication technology assist in tackling this unpredictability proactively and reactively using forecasts, making the system more plannable. This reliance on communication for monitoring and control actions introduces mutual dependencies between power and communication systems. Issues such as incorrect and unavailable data and increased communication latency can lead to erroneous decisions being taken in the power system. These issues impact the state of power system service. Incorrect data can result in imprecise generation predictions, leading to insufficient flexibility to restore a balance between generation and demand and cascading impacts on the power system. This paper discusses the impact of these issues in three power system service contexts: flexibility management, protection and power system restoration and the consequent implications for system resilience. A particular focus is on the states of the power system and the communication-enabled power system services.

articleTitle: Fault-Tolerant Local Recovery with Preprocessing in Multiple Shared Protection
publicationTitle: 2024 14th International Workshop on Resilient Networks Design and Modeling (RNDM)
abstract: In distributed microservice architecture, low latency and high reliability are crucial as they directly impact user experience by ensuring robust service continuity across the network. Function unavailability occurs due to various reasons, and when such failures are detected, the nodes hosting the backup resources can attempt autonomously local recovery, leveraging precomputed recovery policies, without the need for central processor intervention, thereby reducing recovery time. In scenarios involving shared protection with limited recovery capabilities, it is crucial to implement a well-defined policy for local recovery. Such a policy prevents repetitive or infeasible recovery attempts, ensuring effective recovery. This paper considers a local strategy to maximize the residual resilience, where individual nodes decide which function to recover. It hence works as a complement to global recovery to provide prompt recovery, as a first line of defense. This paper hence considers the preparation of priority settings with preprocessing based on the SUPPORTED model. We conduct a comprehensive analysis of the conditions for achieving feasible and optimal local recovery solutions with zero-round communication for one and two failures. Additionally, we formulate the problem as an integer linear programming problem and design a testbed to implement the local recovery algorithm incorporating preprocessing. Our evaluation reveals that the zero-round communication approach emerges as the optimal choice, drastically shortening recovery times to 10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">−6</sup> seconds while maintaining <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathbf{9 8 \%}$</tex> feasibility and perfect optimality for all practical solutions, on average, across two failure scenarios.

articleTitle: Simulation Study on the Impact of Variable SKR and Outdated Information in QKD Networks
publicationTitle: 2024 14th International Workshop on Resilient Networks Design and Modeling (RNDM)
abstract: Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) networks seek to address the challenges of secure communications in postquantum networks. QKD modules are used to ensure secure key rates (SKRs). Due to the generation process, there may be some fluctuations in the key creation rate. In order to decrease the impact of these fluctuations, buffers are used in each link, designated as quantum key pools (QKPs). These QKPs are periodically refilled. Link weights dependent on the QKP filling level are used to calculate the shortest path, applying Dijkstra's algorithm, for key routing. A Software Defined Networking (SDN) architecture is considered. We consider the SKR fluctuations, and we study the impact on the routing performance of outdated QKP filling level information at the controller. Results will show that management traffic can be reduced without compromising the routing performance. However, reducing the frequency update of the link weights will have a negative impact on QKP filling level, but will reduce the controller processing load.

articleTitle: Performability Evaluation of Softwarized Multi-Tenant 5G Architectures with Rejuvenation
publicationTitle: 2024 14th International Workshop on Resilient Networks Design and Modeling (RNDM)
abstract: In this work, we devise a framework designed to evaluate the performability of softwarized multi-tenant <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$5 \mathbf{G}$</tex> architectures, where rejuvenation might be applied. Rejuvenation refers to the procedure of occasionally restarting a software system aimed at counteracting aging-related problems and improving its availability. We utilize queueing theory for a performance characterization, employing an <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M / G / k$</tex> model to embody estimated service times of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$5 \mathbf{G}$</tex> nodes. Conversely, availability modeling is addressed through the Multidimensional Universal Generating Function (MUGF), a recently developed technique particularly beneficial for multi-tenant architectures with numerous sub-elements. Most numerical parameters have been estimated through Open5GS, an open-source platform emulating the softwarized core network of a real 5G network operator.

articleTitle: Impact of Channel Provisioning Strategies in the Transient Resiliency of SuperC+L-band Networks
publicationTitle: 2024 14th International Workshop on Resilient Networks Design and Modeling (RNDM)
abstract: Optical networks are a key building block of today's telecommunications infrastructure. As fundamental limits in spectral efficiency are getting closer, there is a renewed need to cater for more spectrum in these networks to meet the evergrowing capacity requirements. A cost-effective way to achieve this while relying on the existing fiber infrastructure is to exploit the SuperC+L transmission band. However, in these systems, the impact of power transients on the resilience of established services can be significantly higher. This paper introduces a framework to design and simulate the operation of a wideband optical network and to estimate the impact of power transients. Simulation results obtained on a reference transport network highlight the impact of the selected channel provisioning strategies on the resiliency of established services to power transients, providing insight into the trade-off between aggressive (optical margin) provisioning and reduced service impact of transients.

articleTitle: A Tutorial on Reliable Quantum Networks
publicationTitle: 2024 14th International Workshop on Resilient Networks Design and Modeling (RNDM)
abstract: Quantum networks use quantum communication protocols to transmit quantum information (or qubits) between distant quantum processors. This is needed to cope with the limitation regarding available and usable qubits characterizing available quantum processors and realize distributed quantum computing. Unlike classical networks, where information is duplicated and directly transmitted, quantum bits cannot be directly transmitted, so these networks leverage quantum mechanical principles, like entanglement, to enable secure and potentially faster communication. Current quantum networks are primarily research prototypes, and significant engineering challenges remain; reliability is among them. This paper is a tutorial on reliability issues and a simulation of the primary faults in quantum networks envisioned in the current network infrastructures.

articleTitle: Computing Safest $st$-Paths in Backbone Networks: Efficiently Solvable Cases and Fast Heuristics
publicationTitle: 2024 14th International Workshop on Resilient Networks Design and Modeling (RNDM)
abstract: For proper evaluation and optimization of the expected availability of a backbone network service, two related very fundamental modeling and algorithmic questions are the following. 1) Realistically estimate the availability of a given <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$st$</tex>-path for some source and target pair of communicating nodes <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$s$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$t$</tex>, and 2) Find a safest <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$st$</tex>-path. For these, traditional approaches suppose network element failures are independent. In this paper, we show that, by not considering joint failure probabilities, the traditional approaches may misguess the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$st$</tex>-path availabilities and, consequently, the total connection availability, which can lead to more frequent Service Level Agreement (SLA) violations and a financial burden on the Communication Service Provider (CSP). Due to the inconsistent estimations, the supposedly safest paths yielded by these approaches may turn out to be suboptimal. On the positive side, we propose a fast algorithmic approach, that, under some assumptions, returns with a (truly) safest <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$st$</tex>-path accompanied by its exact expected availability. When the aforementioned assumptions do not hold, in our simulations, the proposed algorithmic scheme proved to be a good heuristic, performing at least as well as the traditional method.
